name: Attention is a memory
problem: Why does attention work as retrieval — and why do some heads average instead of choosing?
why: A modern Hopfield network stores patterns as the columns of X and has an energy that the update ξ ← X softmax(βXᵀξ) can only lower. That update is attention, with keys and values X and β = 1/√d. So attention is one step of energy minimisation in an associative memory, and β decides whether that step lands on one stored pattern or an average of many.
symbols: X: stored patterns, one per column — the keys and values
β: inverse temperature; the transformer uses 1/√d
E: the Hopfield energy, lowered by every update
steps: The energy: a log-sum-exp that pulls ξ toward the stored patterns, and a quadratic that keeps it bounded.
The gradient of log-sum-exp is a softmax-weighted sum of the patterns.
The concave–convex procedure sets the quadratic's gradient equal to that one: ξ_new is exactly the weighted sum. The energy cannot rise.
With Q = ξᵀ, K = V = Xᵀ and β = 1/√d this is the same expression.
example: Measured in this app with 32 patterns in 64 dimensions: the two formulas differ by 6.7×10⁻¹⁶; the energy of one query fell from 122.6 to 30.6 over twelve updates and never rose; at β = 0.02 the result mixed 27 patterns, at β = 1/√64 it mixed 1.1 — retrieval in a single step.
deep: Storage capacity is exponential in the dimension, unlike the classical Hopfield network's linear capacity — the reason a modern network can hold far more patterns than it has dimensions. Small β produces metastable states that average many patterns; Ramsauer et al. found heads in trained BERT models at both ends, some retrieving and some averaging.
trap: The equivalence is exact for one update with K = V = X. A transformer projects queries, keys and values separately, so a real attention layer is a Hopfield update in a learned space, not literally a memory over the raw tokens.
question: At small β, what does one Hopfield update return?
answers: A softmax-weighted average of many stored patterns

source.name: Ramsauer et al., Hopfield Networks is All You Need (ICLR 2021)
source.note: Written for this application; measured on the Physics page.
